items.scenarioContext: A teammate gives you critical feedback in a meeting. You feel defensive, but you want to understand the concern.
items.prompt: What is a constructive next step?

options.text: Ask for a specific example and listen before responding.
Agree with every point immediately, even if you are unsure.
Respond with a personal criticism of your teammate.

a.feedback: Asking for an example clarifies the concern and gives you time to respond thoughtfully. You can still disagree after you understand the feedback.

b.feedback: Staying calm can help, but agreeing before you understand may hide important questions or your own boundaries.

c.feedback: A personal attack is likely to escalate the disagreement and move attention away from the feedback itself.

items.followUpReflection: What would help you feel ready to respond to difficult feedback?

items.scenarioContext: You are stuck in traffic and late for an important meeting. You feel your anger rising.
items.prompt: What helps you regulate in this moment?

options.text: Take a few slow breaths and call to say you will be late.
Honk repeatedly and vent angrily at other drivers.
Stew quietly and arrive without saying anything.

a.feedback: Naming the feeling and taking a breath gives you a moment to choose a calmer response, and a quick call manages expectations.

b.feedback: Venting at others rarely changes the traffic and can intensify your own stress.

c.feedback: Noticing the feeling is a start, but staying silent can leave the frustration unprocessed and others unaware.

items.followUpReflection: What small habit helps you reset when plans go off track?

items.scenarioContext: A colleague has been distant and short with you this week.
items.prompt: How do you make sense of this?

options.text: Assume they are upset with you and pull away.
Ask gently if everything is okay, without assuming.
Gossip with others about their mood.

a.feedback: Assuming the cause can harden a misunderstanding before you know what is going on.

b.feedback: Checking in without assuming leaves room for context you do not have, and keeps the relationship open.

c.feedback: Gossip tends to spread assumptions and rarely helps either of you.

items.followUpReflection: When have you misread a situation that later made sense?

items.scenarioContext: A friend repeatedly asks you to cover their shifts with little notice, and you are already overloaded.
items.prompt: How do you respond this time?

options.text: Always say yes to avoid conflict.
Politely say no and suggest an alternative or a future time.
Agree but do it resentfully.

a.feedback: Avoiding conflict by overcommitting can leave you burned out and quietly resentful.

b.feedback: Stating your limit kindly and offering an alternative respects both the friendship and your capacity.

c.feedback: Helping while resentful can build quiet frustration; naming the limit would serve you both better.

items.followUpReflection: What helps you say no without guilt when you need to?

items.scenarioContext: You notice your jaw tightening and your replies getting shorter during a meeting.
items.prompt: What is a helpful first step?

options.text: Pause and name to yourself what you are feeling before you speak.
Push the feeling down and keep going as if nothing is wrong.
Snap at the next person who speaks.

a.feedback: Naming the feeling to yourself creates a small gap between the emotion and your next action.

b.feedback: Pushing feelings down can make them harder to notice and manage later.

c.feedback: Acting on the tension without pausing tends to affect the people around you and the conversation.

items.followUpReflection: What signals does your body give you before you feel upset?

items.scenarioContext: A friend says they are fine but keeps avoiding eye contact and answers briefly.
items.prompt: How do you respond to the mismatch?

options.text: Gently mention what you notice and ask if they want to talk.
Take the fine at face value and drop it.
Insist that they are clearly lying about being fine.

a.feedback: Noticing the mismatch and offering space respects their choice while showing you care.

b.feedback: Taking fine at face value can miss a signal, though some people do need space.

c.feedback: Calling someone a liar can feel unsafe and may close the conversation.

items.followUpReflection: How do you usually show someone you are ready to listen?

items.scenarioContext: You are excited and nervous about a big move. Some days you feel both at once.
items.prompt: What is a helpful way to understand this?

options.text: Name both feelings and note what each one is telling you.
Decide you must feel only one thing and push the other away.
Wait until the feelings sort themselves out before acting.

a.feedback: Mixed feelings often carry useful information; naming both can reduce their pull.

b.feedback: Forcing one feeling away can make the other harder to understand.

c.feedback: Waiting for feelings to settle can help sometimes, but it may delay choices you can make now.

items.followUpReflection: When have two feelings pointed you toward a decision?

items.scenarioContext: A peer's report has a few gaps, and you need to raise them before a deadline.
items.prompt: How do you share the feedback?

options.text: Describe the specific gaps and ask how you can help close them.
Rewrite the whole report yourself without telling them.
Point out the gaps in front of the whole team.

a.feedback: Specific, private feedback with an offer to help is easier to act on.

b.feedback: Quietly redoing the work can create confusion and takes away their chance to improve.

c.feedback: Public criticism can feel humiliating and rarely improves the work.

items.followUpReflection: What makes feedback easier for you to hear and use?

items.scenarioContext: In a group chat, two friends start arguing and tag you to pick a side.

options.text: Say you would rather not take sides here and suggest talking one-to-one.
Jump in and back the friend you agree with most.
Leave the chat without saying anything.

a.feedback: Naming your boundary and offering a calmer channel keeps the relationship open without fuelling the argument.

b.feedback: Picking a side can deepen the split and pull you into a fight you did not choose.

c.feedback: Leaving avoids the clash but may leave the group without a calmer option.

items.followUpReflection: How do you stay connected when people disagree strongly?

items.scenarioContext: You realise you snapped at a teammate earlier and the mood is tense.
items.prompt: What is a constructive next step?

options.text: Apologise for the tone, explain briefly, and ask how they are doing.
Pretend nothing happened and hope it blows over.
Blame your stress and say they should not be so sensitive.

a.feedback: A specific apology that owns the tone and checks in repairs trust faster than silence.

b.feedback: Letting it blow over can leave the teammate unsure whether it will happen again.

c.feedback: Deflecting and calling them sensitive can make the other person feel dismissed.

items.followUpReflection: What does a repair look like after a tense moment for you?

items.scenarioContext: You receive a blunt message from a client that feels unfair. Your heart is racing.
items.prompt: What do you do before replying?

options.text: Wait, reread the message, and draft a calm reply.
Fire back an angry reply right away.
Ignore the message and hope they forget.

a.feedback: Pausing and drafting lets you respond to the issue rather than the sting.

b.feedback: An immediate angry reply usually escalates a conflict.

c.feedback: Ignoring a work message can leave the problem to grow.

items.followUpReflection: What helps you cool down before you write back?

items.scenarioContext: Under a tight deadline, a colleague asks you a long question. You feel irritation rising.

options.text: Say you want to help and suggest a short time to talk after the deadline.
Snap that you do not have time for this right now.
Sigh loudly and answer with one word.

a.feedback: Naming the time limit honestly and offering a later slot respects both your focus and their need.

b.feedback: Snapping can damage trust even when the pressure is real.

c.feedback: A sigh and a one-word answer sends frustration without solving the request.

items.followUpReflection: How can you protect your focus without shutting people out?

items.scenarioContext: A close friend cancels plans at the last minute for the second time.
items.prompt: How do you make sense of it?

options.text: Tell them you feel let down and ask what is going on for them.
Assume they do not care about you and go quiet.
Post about being ditched online.

a.feedback: Sharing your feeling and asking about theirs checks an assumption before it hardens.

b.feedback: Assuming the worst can turn a busy week into a story about not being valued.

c.feedback: Posting publicly can embarrass your friend and rarely helps the friendship.

items.followUpReflection: What is a fair way to check a story you are telling yourself?

items.scenarioContext: A customer speaks sharply to you over a delay that was not your fault.

options.text: Acknowledge their frustration and explain what you can do next.
Tell them it is not your fault and walk away.
Match their sharp tone to show you will not be pushed around.

a.feedback: Acknowledging their frustration first usually lowers the heat and lets you move to solutions.

b.feedback: Being defensive is understandable, but it can leave the customer without a path forward.

c.feedback: Matching their tone tends to turn a service problem into a conflict.

items.followUpReflection: What helps you see the person behind a sharp tone?

items.scenarioContext: A new acquaintance asks for your home address shortly after meeting you.

options.text: Say you prefer not to share that yet and offer another way to stay in touch.
Give the address to avoid seeming rude.
Get angry and accuse them of prying.

a.feedback: A calm limit plus an alternative keeps the connection without over-sharing.

b.feedback: Sharing personal details to avoid awkwardness can leave you less safe than you would like.

c.feedback: Anger signals a limit, but a calm explanation is easier for the other person to hear.

items.followUpReflection: How do you decide what personal information to share?

items.scenarioContext: A family member keeps pushing you toward a career choice you are unsure about.
items.prompt: How do you handle the pressure?

options.text: Thank them for caring and say you need time to decide for yourself.
Agree to keep the peace and then resent it.
Shut down the conversation every time it comes up.

a.feedback: Acknowledging their care while claiming your own decision keeps the relationship and your agency.

b.feedback: Agreeing under pressure can build resentment and delay a choice that is yours.

c.feedback: Shutting down protects you in the moment but may not reduce the pressure over time.

items.followUpReflection: What helps you hold a limit with someone close to you?
